Menstealers
MEN-steel-erz
n. pl. (kidnappers; those who seize and sell human beings)
From men and stealer, rendering Greek andrapodistes, a slave-dealer, one who enslaves a free man. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's list of those the law is made for.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine. Paul is explaining the proper use of the law, which is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, and his catalogue runs in the order of the Decalogue — murderers of fathers and mothers against the fifth commandment, manslayers against the sixth, whoremongers and the defilers against the seventh, menstealers against the eighth, liars and perjured persons against the ninth. Manstealing is the eighth commandment's worst form: not the theft of a man's goods but the theft of the man. The Mosaic law made it capital without qualification, and without regard to what became of him afterwards: he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death. And Paul closes the list by measuring all of it against the gospel: according to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one that steals and carries away a man or men; a kidnapper; in Scripture, named among those contrary to sound doctrine.

expand to see more

MAN-STEALER, n. One that steals and carries away a man or men; a kidnapper.

KIDNAP, v.t. To steal and carry away any person whatever, whether man, woman or child.

LAWLESS, a. Not subject to law; unrestrained by law; contrary to law; illegal.

SOUND, a. Firm; strong; valid; solid; well-founded; as sound doctrine.

DECALOGUE, n. The ten commandments or precepts given by God to Moses at mount Sinai.

Key Scripture

1Ti 1:10 — "For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;"

1Ti 1:9 — "Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,"

Exo 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

1Ti 1:11 — "According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust."

Modern Corruption

The Bible is said to sanction slavery, and the texts that condemn its foundation are passed over; Exodus makes manstealing a capital crime and Paul lists menstealers among those whose trade is contrary to sound doctrine.

expand to see more

The chattel slavery of the Atlantic trade rested entirely on manstealing: men and women seized, sold, and held as property who had never been captives of war, debtors, or convicts. Scripture pronounces the death penalty on the first link of that chain and names the traders among the lawless. This was not a nineteenth-century discovery. The abolitionists argued it from these texts, and the defenders of the trade had to work around them, which is the usual position of those defending an institution the Bible condemns at its root.

The regulation of servitude within Israel — release in the seventh year, freedom for a maimed servant, refuge for a runaway rather than his return, sabbath rest extended to servants, and the jubilee — belongs to a different institution and a different world from the one these texts condemn. And the New Testament's trajectory runs one way: Paul sends Onesimus back as a brother beloved, tells servants who may be made free to use it rather, commands masters to remember they have a Master in heaven, and places menstealers in a list with murderers. The dictionary names the trade by the name Scripture gives it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek andrapodistes (G405), a slave-dealer, a manstealer; anomos (G459), lawless; Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal.

expand to see more

Greek andrapodistes (G405) — an enslaver, a manstealer; the one occurrence, 1 Timothy 1:10.

Greek anomos (G459) — lawless, without law; the law is made for the lawless.

Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound or healthy; contrary to sound doctrine.

Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal; he that stealeth a man.

Hebrew muwth (H4191) — to die, to be put to death; he shall surely be put to death.

Usage

"“for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons” — the single occurrence."

"“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” — a capital crime under the law."

"“contrary to sound doctrine” — the category Paul assigns it to."
